stories.headline: Congo's Confirmed Ebola Cases Surpass 9,000 as Containment Efforts Falter
stories.summary:
Confirmed cases in Congo's Ebola outbreak have passed 9,000, with more than 4,300 deaths, according to government figures released Tuesday. The Health Ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths, meaning the death toll is approaching half the number of confirmed cases. The latest report recorded 88 new cases and warned that "community transmission remains a concern."

The outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. It now affects 65 health zones across seven provinces, creating new hot spots as it reaches more communities. Officials say confirmed cases account for only about a third of all cases, with many going undetected, and a large share of deaths are occurring outside treatment centers.

Containment has been hampered by fighting between government forces and rebel groups, widespread disregard for health precautions, heavy population movement, and shortages of medical supplies and treatment centers. The outbreak has surpassed Congo's 16 previous outbreaks in scale and is on track to exceed the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, which killed 11,000 people. Last week Kenya became the second country after Uganda to report an Ebola case imported from Congo, deepening fears of cross-border spread.

"I feel that the government is overwhelmed by events," said Samuel Buju, a resident of Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, one of the hot spots. He said the government needs to fully shoulder its responsibilities in the response.

stories.headline: Argentina Files Legal Claim Against UK Over Falklands Oil Exploration
stories.summary:
Argentina has begun legal action to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields north of the Falkland Islands, escalating a sovereignty row with Britain. Buenos Aires lodged a request with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, based in Hamburg, seeking to block activity it says the UK authorized "illegally." Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said Argentina is asking the tribunal for orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits.

The filing comes about two weeks after President Javier Milei demanded the scrapping of the Sea Lion oilfield project, a venture involving Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum. Milei has also threatened economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil near the islands. Sea Lion, about 130 miles from the Falklands, holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels and is expected to begin pumping in 2028, potentially bringing large revenues to the islands' roughly 3,500 inhabitants.

UK Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran told the House of Commons the government would "do whatever it takes" to support the islanders, accused Argentina of "economic coercion," and announced new protections for companies operating there. She said the tribunal application does not invalidate licenses or require lawful development to stop. The UK maintains Sea Lion is lawful and regulated by the islands' government, while Argentina argues the marine environment of disputed areas is protected under international law. The dispute comes more than 40 years after Britain expelled Argentine forces that invaded the islands.

stories.headline: Carney Heads to Alberta Days Before Independence Referendum
stories.summary:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is traveling to Alberta days before residents of the oil-rich province vote in a referendum on whether to remain in Canada or seek independence.

The vote is a major test of national unity, given Alberta's central role in Canada's energy sector and economy. Carney's visit signals the federal government's concern about the outcome and its effort to make the case for remaining in the federation.

The result could carry significant consequences for Canadian politics, energy markets and relations between Ottawa and the western provinces. Further details on the visit and the campaign were not available in the initial report.

stories.headline: Ex-Gang Boss Sentenced to At Least 40 Years for Orchestrating Tupac Shakur's Murder
stories.summary:
Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, was sentenced Tuesday to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas. A jury found him guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon. Davis said at the hearing, "I'm gonna appeal this case for sure."

Prosecutors argued that Davis did not fire the gun but was the ringleader of the group that carried out the drive-by shooting on Sept. 7, 1996, and that he supplied the weapon. Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" about his role. The conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

Key evidence was Davis' own words, including repeated public acknowledgments that he was in the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired. He described his role in a secret 2008 police interview in exchange for protection from prosecution, then elaborated in his 2019 memoir, which voided that agreement and allowed the interview to be used at trial.

Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, and brother, Maurice Shakur, asked for the longest possible sentence. Judge Carli Kierny told Davis, "You don't get to take a man from his family," adding that the world never forgot Shakur's death. Shakur was 25 and had sold more than 75 million records.

stories.headline: Update: Cyberattacks Disrupt Refrigeration at Hundreds of European Supermarkets, Ahold Delhaize Takes Websites Offline
stories.summary:
French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected by cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged that the attack "touches the heart of our food security," calling it "a wake-up call for everyone." The Paris prosecutor's office said its cybercrime unit is investigating the attack, including the extent of damage from spoiled food and reports of fires.

Groupement Mousquetaires, which operates more than 4,000 stores across Europe, said 300 of its Intermarché and Netto stores were affected, and some refrigerated and frozen display cases remained out of service Tuesday. Cooperative U said 80 of its 2,000 stores were hit, and its CEO, Dominique Schelcher, called the attack "unprecedented, extremely serious, and unacceptable." Carrefour and Monoprix stores were also affected.

The new development is a second incident. Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates Albert Heijn, Delhaize and Stop & Shop in the United States, said it was working to restore systems it shut down after what it called a security issue. Websites for several brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Albert Heijn, remained offline Tuesday, though stores were open. The company said it had no evidence that customer or employee data had been stolen.

Danish supplier Danfoss, which provided the refrigeration management software, said most affected systems were older products that no longer received security updates. The company said it has long advised customers to keep systems updated and to operate behind a firewall. Investigators have not publicly identified those responsible.

stories.headline: Update: Trump's Russian Diesel Deal and Senate Map Strain Republicans as Vance Invokes Defense Production Act for Texas Refinery
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance announced Tuesday that the administration will invoke the Defense Production Act to expand the Delek refinery in Tyler, Texas, to boost production of commercial and military-grade fuel. Vance made the announcement while campaigning for Republican candidates, as diesel prices remain above $6 per gallon and fuel costs have become a political liability ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

Separately, opposition to President Trump's Oct. 9 deal with Vladimir Putin, under which sanctions on Russian energy are waived to allow roughly 2.5 million tons of Russian diesel into the U.S. and global markets, has grown in Congress. Six Republican senators, including Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn, signed a letter calling the deal "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies," and a separate bipartisan group urged him to withdraw. The administration says the deal will lower costs for Americans; critics, including energy analysts, question whether it will deliver relief at the pump.

The political backdrop is increasingly difficult for the GOP. Polling shows Republicans competitive in Maine, Alaska and Minnesota but defending tighter races in Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and Nebraska. Trump traveled to Alaska on Tuesday to support an incumbent senator, and a Senate Republican-allied super PAC plans to spend an additional $8 million to help Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts against independent Dan Osborn. Two major House Republican super PACs are pulling money from some incumbents' races.

Republicans have argued that high energy prices stem from the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and that the administration is acting to ease them. Democrats say the diesel deal rewards Moscow and that the White House is scrambling because of Trump's low approval ratings.

stories.headline: Mauritius Declares Curfew After Worst Riots Since 1999
stories.summary:
Prime Minister Navinchandra Ramgoolam of Mauritius declared a curfew after the Indian Ocean island nation experienced its worst riots since 1999. The unrest is a significant disruption for a country best known for its beach resorts and tourism-dependent economy.

The initial report did not detail the cause of the riots, casualty figures or the curfew's duration. The 1999 riots, the last comparable episode, were a major moment of civil unrest in the country, which has otherwise been regarded as one of Africa's more stable democracies.

The curfew is likely to affect tourists and the hospitality sector, which is central to the island's economy. Further details on the scope of the unrest and the government's response are expected as the situation develops.

stories.headline: Fed's Williams Says One More Rate Hike Appropriate This Year
stories.summary:
Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said one more interest-rate increase is appropriate this year. Williams, a permanent voter on the Federal Open Market Committee and a close ally of the Fed chair, spoke to Bloomberg off camera in New York.

He also said he does not expect the central bank to need to raise rates again in 2027. The comment suggests Fed officials view the current tightening cycle as nearing its end, even as energy prices remain elevated because of the Iran war and disruptions to fuel supplies.

The remarks arrive amid inflation pressures from high diesel and oil prices, which have become a central political issue before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Markets will watch for whether other Fed officials echo Williams's outlook.

stories.headline: Ukraine's Former Top General Says Russia's Offensive Ability Is 'Broken'
stories.summary:
Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief, told the BBC in an exclusive interview that Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by inflicting heavy losses on Russian forces. It was his first interview since he was forced from his post in the summer. He said Moscow's overall losses in the war are six times higher than Ukraine's, and up to 11 times higher if only deaths are counted.

Syrskyi said Russia seized only 61 square kilometres in the first six months of 2026, which he cited as evidence that the front has stabilised. The Institute for the Study of War has reported a similar trend, saying Moscow lost more territory than it took in September. Neither side officially releases casualty figures, and Ukraine's claim of record Russian losses in September cannot be independently verified. UK intelligence estimates Russia has lost around half a million men killed since 2022, while the Center for Strategic and International Studies believes Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.

Syrskyi was dismissed after a public dispute between President Volodymyr Zelensky and then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who accused the army of blocking his initiatives. Zelensky first fired Fedorov, but mass street protests then forced him to remove Syrskyi too, and Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43, replaced him. Syrskyi rejected criticism that he was too "old school" and pushed back on soldiers' allegations that they were ordered to hold positions when nearly surrounded. He said Fedorov's procurement had favoured drones while neglecting items such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes.

stories.headline: Taliban Suspend BBC FM Radio Transmissions Across Afghanistan
stories.summary:
Afghanistan's Taliban government has suspended the transmission of BBC broadcasts from FM radio sites across the country. Ministry of Information and Culture spokesman Khubaib Ghufran said the suspension was due to "repeated violations" by the BBC, without elaborating, and that it would last "for the time being."

The BBC has been the only international news organisation broadcasting inside Afghanistan since two US outlets were banned in 2022. It reaches more than 20% of the adult population each week, including educational programming for girls who have been barred from secondary schools. The broadcaster said millions of Afghans rely on it for accurate news and that it is working with the authorities to resolve the situation.

The BBC said it continues to report in Pashto, Dari and English on shortwave and medium wave radio, online and by satellite. The Taliban keep a tight grip on media since retaking power in 2021: music is not broadcast, women appear less on screen, and women no longer appear on air alongside men. Social media remains partly accessible, but power shortages, high costs and low literacy limit access, which makes radio an important source of information. The BBC's Afghan service has operated since 1981.

stories.headline: Update: NATO Commander Vows to 'Break' Russian Warfighting System if Alliance Is Attacked
stories.summary:
NATO's top military commander, US Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, warned on Monday that the alliance would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, he said, "Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us." He said this covers not only an attacking force but everything that supports, sustains and controls it.

Grynkewich, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe, outlined a three-part strategy of "blocking, blunting and breaking" enemy forces. He stressed that NATO is a defensive alliance but is ready to respond decisively to an assault on any of its 32 members. "If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said, adding that any attack would prove "utterly futile."

The remarks come amid heightened tensions following drone incursions and suspected sabotage that European countries link to Moscow. European officials accuse Russia of a hybrid campaign of sabotage, arson and cyberattacks. In 2025, Russian drones entered Polish airspace during a large attack on Ukraine, prompting NATO to launch Operation Eastern Sentry to reinforce its eastern flank. The new element is the specific public warning delivered at the Warsaw forum.

stories.headline: Where the US Midterm Elections Will Be Won and Lost
stories.summary:
Americans vote on 3 November in midterm elections that will shape the rest of Donald Trump's presidency. Republicans control both chambers of Congress, and the main contests are for the House of Representatives and the Senate. Thousands of other races are also on the ballot at various levels of government.

Trump's approval rating is a key factor, sitting at about 37% according to Silver Bulletin, down from just over 50% at the start of his second term. It fell below 40% after the US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran at the end of February. At the same point in his first term it was 43%, and Joe Biden's was 40%; in both cases the president's party lost the House but held the Senate. Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers and are targeting states Republicans have won consistently.

Republicans hold 218 House seats, the exact number needed for control, plus one independent who votes with them. Cook Political Report rates just 21 districts as toss-ups, 15 held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If Democrats win five of those plus 28 districts rated likely or leaning Democratic, they would take the House. Since 1934 the president's party has lost an average of 27 House seats in midterms. In the Senate, Republicans hold 53 seats to the Democrats' 45 plus two independents who vote with them, giving Republicans a somewhat firmer grip.

stories.headline: One Dead, Several Hurt on Goliath Rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia
stories.summary:
One person died and several others were injured in an incident on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles from Atlanta. The Cobb County Police Department said it was investigating the fatality. Police did not name the ride, but aerial footage showed the Goliath coaster stopped midway while workers helped riders off.

Officials have not said how the person died or how the others were hurt, and the victim has not been identified. Witnesses told local outlet 11 Alive that a man came loose from his seat, struck the coaster and other riders, and fell onto the roof of a nearby haunted house attraction. A couple said park workers had checked their harnesses before the ride began. The BBC has not verified these accounts.

Six Flags said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and is cooperating with the investigation. The company also said it temporarily closed similar attractions across its parks "out of an abundance of caution." Goliath opened in 2006, stands 200 feet tall, and reaches speeds of up to 70 mph.

The death comes weeks after a Six Flags park in southern California said it would close the X2 coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from riding it. Six Flags said that ride had passed safety tests but was being retired because it was "the right thing to do." Six Flags is North America's largest amusement park operator, with 20 amusement parks.

stories.headline: Ex-President Joseph Kabila Named Leader of New DR Congo Rebel Coalition
stories.summary:
Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila has been named leader of a new rebel coalition seeking to oust the government of President Felix Tshisekedi. The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it would coordinate "resistance forces" to end "tyranny" and would pursue that goal "by all means, including force." The group was unveiled Monday at a press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma, the largest city in eastern DR Congo, which M23 rebels have controlled since last year.

The announcement is the clearest sign yet of Kabila's direct involvement in an armed movement, a year after he was sentenced to death in absentia for treason. He had previously denied links to M23. M23 leader Sultani Makenga will serve as one of Kabila's four deputies, and the other three also come from the AFC-M23 alliance.

The launch followed a speech days earlier in which Kabila accused Tshisekedi's government of ignoring his peace proposals, undermining constitutional rule, mismanaging the economy and making arbitrary arrests of opponents and officers. The government has not commented publicly on the coalition or the accusations.

Kabila ruled from 2001 until January 2019, when Tshisekedi took office after a disputed election. The two were once allies before falling out, and Kabila went into exile in 2023 before returning to Goma last year. More than 100 militia groups operate in eastern DR Congo. The UN and Western governments accuse Rwanda of backing M23, which Rwanda denies. Tshisekedi said in May that elections due in 2028 might not be held because of the conflict.

stories.headline: Hungarian Parliament Scraps Orban-Era Anti-LGBTQ Measures as EU Releases Frozen Funds
stories.summary:
Hungary's parliament voted Tuesday to amend child protection laws, scrapping measures that stigmatized gay and transgender people. The 2021 Child Protection Law, passed by Viktor Orban's Fidesz majority, banned the "portrayal or promotion of homosexuality or transgenderism" and affected laws on education and assembly. LGBTQ and human rights activists welcomed the change but called for further reforms of Orban-era laws.

The vote is part of a package of laws from the government of Prime Minister Peter Magyar, whose Tisza party won in April and holds the same two-thirds majority Fidesz once had. Minutes after the vote, Budapest said the EU had agreed to release 4.2bn euros in funds frozen during the last years of the Fidesz government. The European Commission had said last month that Hungary addressed a number of rule-of-law breaches affecting the EU budget, and urged readmitting it to Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.

Tamas Dombos of the Hatter Society said his group had fought the law for five years, though he said problems remain and "we are still knocking on a closed door" on other issues. Magyar's party has softened the legislation without presenting itself as fully liberal on equality, and he avoided gay and transgender rights during his campaign for fear of alienating right-wing voters. Child protection had been central to both parties' images, and it became a liability for Orban after his government supported the pardon of a children's home official who covered up abuse.

stories.headline: Super El Nino Sets New Records, Strengthening to 'Unprecedented Levels'
stories.summary:
El Nino has continued to strengthen to what some scientists call "unprecedented levels," weeks before its expected peak in December. Australia's Bureau of Meteorology said average weekly sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific have reached their highest level on record. This follows a record daily sea surface temperature in the central-eastern Pacific set in September, which exceeded the mark from the very strong 2015 event.

Temperatures above 30C have been recorded for the first time in parts of the tropical Pacific, along with record anomalies and exceptional subsurface warmth. Forecasters in Australia and the US now use a Relative Ocean El Nino Index to account for background ocean warming from climate change. By that measure, current levels exceed the record-breaking December 2015 peak. Dr Zeke Hausfather of Berkeley Earth said, "We are currently witnessing an El Nino event that is unprecedented in the historical record."

The warmth extends well beyond the tropical region normally monitored, and is more widespread than in the 1972-73, 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 events. The World Meteorological Organization says there is no evidence that climate change is making El Nino events stronger or more frequent, though this remains an active research area. El Nino releases extra ocean heat into the atmosphere, and combined with human-driven warming it is expected to make 2026 one of the warmest years on record, with high temperatures likely to continue into 2027. The most widespread impacts are expected later this year and into 2027.

stories.headline: Update: Ships Sunk in New Drone Attacks Off Bulgaria as Prime Minister Summons Russian Ambassador
stories.summary:
A merchant ship has sunk after drones struck two vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. One ship went down 17 nautical miles east of Krapets, and one crew member was saved. The second, Ukrainian-owned and Maltese-flagged vessel, the Chelsea 3, was hit by three drones 18 nautical miles from the town of Byala. All 15 crew were rescued, and five were treated for minor injuries.

Radev convened an emergency security meeting and summoned Russian ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova. He said there was no conclusive evidence of blame on either side, but that "the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation." Mitrofanova reportedly told him she had no information from Russia's defense ministry about the attacks and suggested a third-party provocation. Radev, who took office this summer and has rejected suggestions that he is pro-Russian, said he would speak with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

The attacks follow a similar incident on October 6, when two commercial ships were hit in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. One of them, the Alfa Watan, sank, and all 10 crew, including nine Syrians, are presumed dead. Radev had earlier asked NATO and the EU for technical help in investigating those strikes.

Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for the latest attacks. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Black Sea was becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable." Moscow has not commented publicly. It says it targets ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports, while Kyiv and its European allies say grain and other civilian cargo vessels are being hit.

stories.headline: Update: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Escalate as Riyadh Airport Death Toll Reaches 13
stories.summary:
The death toll from the Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport and another facility has risen to 13, according to the latest reporting. Saturday's attack was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since May 2015. US and Saudi officials blame Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, who had not commented on the strike. The Saudi capital was hit by multiple attacks over the weekend.

The strikes come amid escalating fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government. The Houthis have also been fighting pro-government forces over Yemen's Red Sea coast. Security analysts say the group's precision strikes and guerrilla tactics have made it difficult for Saudi forces to gain the upper hand.

BBC analysis says the physical damage from the attacks can be repaired quickly, but the kingdom's reputation for stability is taking a battering. Experts also note that US military assistance, including shuttle tankers and pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, has allowed Gulf oil exports to rebound.

The attacks sit within the wider US-Iran war and the question of how Washington and Riyadh respond. The Houthi campaign has put new focus on Yemen's long-running civil war, whose humanitarian toll continues to mount.

stories.headline: Katie Zacharia to Hold First White House Press Briefing as New Press Secretary
stories.summary:
Katie Zacharia begins her term as White House press secretary, with an introductory news conference set for Tuesday at 9:30 a.m. President Trump announced the start date on Sunday, saying she would begin on Columbus Day. Her debut ends a weeks-long stretch without a permanent press secretary at the podium.

Zacharia previously worked for one of Trump's companies and built her profile through appearances on conservative-leaning talk shows. Critics note that she has amplified right-wing conspiracy theories. Supporters of the president view her as a loyal communicator who will advance his message directly to the public.

The briefing comes as the Justice Department investigates the five television networks that make up the White House TV press pool, following the suspension of pool coverage. How the new press secretary handles questions on that probe, and on the administration's relationship with the press corps, will be closely watched. The briefing also lands weeks before the midterm elections.

stories.headline: Update: India 'Cockroach' Party Leaders Detained After Entering Barricaded Delhi Protest Site
stories.summary:
Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party were detained early Tuesday after entering the heavily guarded Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi. They chanted slogans demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls. Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared video of Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police after climbing over barricades while holding the Indian flag.

The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar would no longer be a designated protest venue, naming three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission. Ranka said the site was de-notified 30 minutes after the party asked police for a protest date. Opponents of Prime Minister Narendra Modi allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.

Over the weekend, police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists, and closed metro stations amid a heavy deployment of police and paramilitary forces. Opposition parties also marched in Delhi on Monday. The detained leaders said they would not back down.
